identity.title: LLM-SR: Scientific Equation Discovery via Programming with Large Language Models

problem.claim: Discovering insightful scientific equations from data requires navigating extremely large combinatorial hypothesis spaces.

gap.claim: Existing symbolic-regression methods often neglect scientists’ domain-specific prior knowledge and use limited expression-tree representations that constrain search and expressiveness.

contributions.claim: LLM-SR represents equations as programs and combines LLM-generated scientific priors with evolutionary search and parameter optimization.
The authors evaluate LLM-SR on four benchmark problems spanning scientific domains including physics and biology, designed to simulate discovery while preventing LLM recitation.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors present LLM-SR as a novel approach using LLM scientific knowledge and code-generation capabilities to discover equations from data.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that LLM-SR discovers physically accurate equations and significantly outperforms state-of-the-art symbolic-regression baselines, particularly on out-of-domain tests.
The authors report that incorporating scientific priors enables more efficient equation-space exploration than the baselines.

narrative_sequence.summary: Scientific equations describe complex natural phenomena, but discovering them from data involves a very large hypothesis space.
The abstract identifies insufficient use of domain knowledge and restricted expression-tree representations in symbolic regression.
LLM-SR treats equations as programs; an LLM proposes equation skeletons from scientific knowledge, while evolutionary search and data-based parameter optimization refine them.
Across four domain-diverse benchmarks designed to limit recitation, the authors report stronger physical-equation discovery and more efficient exploration, especially out of domain.

source_observation.claim: The approach explicitly links LLM-generated equation skeletons to subsequent data-based parameter optimization and evolutionary search.

lessons.interpretation: Separating structural proposal from parameter fitting can make a large scientific search problem more tractable while retaining domain-informed structure.
lessons.application: For a scientific discovery method, define which component proposes hypothesis structure and which component fits or tests its parameters, then evaluate their interaction.
lessons.exception: This decomposition may be unsuitable when the target structure and parameters must be inferred jointly or when domain priors are unreliable.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the four benchmark tasks, baseline identities, evaluation metrics, or the quantitative meaning of “significantly outperform.”
It does not provide the conditions or measurements underlying the claims of physical accuracy and more efficient exploration.
The abstract does not establish whether the reported advantages generalize beyond the selected benchmarks or out-of-domain settings.
